name: Shrugs / trap training
lead: Shrugs and trapezius training are resistance exercises in which the shoulders are raised against a load, used to build the upper trapezius muscle. In looksmaxxing discussion they are mentioned as a way to make the neck look thicker by building the muscles at its base.

Available research on shrug-type exercises concerns muscle activation and neck-pain rehabilitation rather than appearance. An electromyography study in women with chronic neck muscle pain measured activation of neck and shoulder muscles during selected strengthening exercises [1], and another evaluated muscle activity during a standardized shoulder resistance training bout in novices [2].
infobox: No appearance studies; some EMG studies

paras: A physical therapy study used surface electromyography to measure neck and shoulder muscle activity in 12 women with chronic trapezius myalgia during selected strengthening exercises [1]. A separate study in novice trainees evaluated muscle activity across a standardized shoulder resistance session [2]. Neither assessed changes in neck appearance.

One forum poster reported apparent height gain of about half a centimetre after heavy shrugs and asked whether it was real growth or improved posture [3]. The thread excerpt available does not include replies, and no study has measured height change from shrugs.
No studies found on shrugs for cosmetic neck thickness or height. Electromyography studies of shoulder and neck exercises exist in pain rehabilitation and novice training populations [1][2].

lore.intro: Shrugs are mentioned in forums as a trap exercise connected to neck and posture claims [3].

claims.believers: One poster reported about 0.5 cm of apparent gain after heavy shrugs and wondered whether it was growth or posture [3].
claims.experts: No published studies have examined height change from shrug exercises.

quick.overview:
Shrugs raise the shoulders against weight to train the upper trapezius. In looksmaxxing talk the muscle is linked to a thicker-looking neck.

Research exists on muscle activation during shoulder and neck exercises, but none on appearance.
quick.mechanism: Resistance on shoulder elevation works the upper trapezius; electromyography studies measure this activation in specific populations.
quick.risks: No harms are documented in the available sources. Height-gain claims from shrugs have not been studied.
